anti_overlap: GitHub Contents API SHA concurrency and retry semantics — covered by fd-git-api-concurrency
Webhook delivery ordering and force-push handling — covered by fd-webhook-delivery-reliability
Periodic poll reconciliation and drift correction — covered by fd-filesync-reconciliation-coverage
Sync scope and binary file exclusion policy — covered by fd-sync-scope-safety
decision_lens: A three-way merge is only as correct as its ancestor — if the AncestorStore returns a stale or wrong ancestor version, the merge produces a result that neither side intended, and the system reports success while silently corrupting the file.
focus: Reviews the three-way merge strategy via AncestorStore for correctness, edge cases in text-based conflict detection, ancestor staleness, and the operational path from dead-lettered conflicts to user resolution.
name: fd-three-way-merge-correctness
persona: You are a version control systems engineer who has implemented and debugged merge algorithms in production SCM tools, including the specific failure modes where a nominally clean three-way merge produces semantically incorrect output because the ancestor was not the true common ancestor of both branches.
review_areas: Verify the design specifies what constitutes the ancestor in the AncestorStore: it should be the last version that both the local filesystem and GitHub agreed on — if interop writes a file to GitHub and then the user edits locally before interop has confirmed the write, the stored ancestor is stale and the three-way merge will incorrectly classify the local edit as a conflict

Check whether the merge algorithm handles the case where the local and GitHub versions are identical to the ancestor — this is the most common case (one side changed, the other is at the ancestor) and must produce a clean merge without invoking the user-facing conflict path

Assess the design's handling of concurrent edits to non-overlapping regions of the same file: a true three-way merge should auto-resolve non-overlapping line-range changes without surfacing a conflict, but a naive diff-based approach may produce false conflicts when both sides add content at the same line offset (e.g., both append a new section at the end of a file)

Confirm the AncestorStore update protocol: when is the ancestor updated after a successful sync? If the ancestor is updated before the write is confirmed on both sides, a subsequent failure leaves an incorrect ancestor that will cause future merges to produce wrong results

Validate the conflict UX path described in Open Question 4: the brainstorm says conflicts are dead-lettered to SyncJournal and resolved in Phase 5 via MCP server — but this means a conflict can silently block future syncs of the same file until Phase 5 ships, and the user may not know the file is in a conflicted state without actively querying the SyncJournal

Check whether the merge algorithm is specified for known content types: markdown files have structure (headings, lists, code blocks) that a line-based diff may split incorrectly — a line-based merge that splits a code block across the conflict boundary produces syntactically invalid output that the system would then sync to both sides

severity_examples.condition: When the ancestor is recorded at write-initiation time rather than at write-confirmation time (i.e., after both the Contents API PUT returns 200 and the local file update is complete)
severity_examples.scenario: The AncestorStore records the ancestor as the version interop last wrote, but the user edits the file locally while interop's write to GitHub is in-flight and not yet confirmed — the next sync uses the pre-write ancestor, classifies both the in-flight write and the local edit as diverging from a stale base, and produces a merge that silently drops one side's content

severity_examples.condition: When the merge algorithm uses a strict line-based diff that treats same-position insertions as conflicts rather than a smarter algorithm that can sequence independent insertions
severity_examples.scenario: Both the user locally and a collaborator on GitHub append a new section to the same markdown file at the same end-of-file location — the three-way merge sees both sides adding content at the same line offset, reports a conflict, and dead-letters the event rather than producing a merge that includes both appended sections in document order

severity_examples.condition: When the conflict state for a file does not trigger a user-visible notification and does not block the user from continuing to edit the file locally while the conflict persists
severity_examples.scenario: A file enters a conflict state and is dead-lettered to the SyncJournal — subsequent local edits to the same file continue generating sync events, but the adapter skips the file because it is in conflict state — three days later, the user has made 15 additional local edits that are not on GitHub, and the SyncJournal has accumulated 15 unresolved entries with no user notification

success_hints: The design precisely defines the ancestor invariant as the version that both sides last confirmed as their shared baseline, updated only after successful writes on both sides. The conflict detection distinguishes overlapping edits from same-offset independent insertions. The AncestorStore update is transactional with the write confirmation. The conflict user-notification path is specified even for Phase 4, even if the resolution UI is deferred to Phase 5.
task_context: The brainstorm proposes using AncestorStore for three-way merge when both local filesystem and GitHub have diverged from the last known common state. The ConflictResolver dead-letters unresolvable conflicts to SyncJournal. Phase 5 (MCP server) will expose conflict resolution tooling. The brainstorm uses the Notion adapter as a reference pattern for how three-way merge is expected to work.
